title: Open and close an attempt on the claim and release paths
description:
Objective: put the attempt record on the real lifecycle so every subsequent rule has something to fence against.

Deliverable: packages/moe-daemon/src/tools/claimNextTask.ts opens an attempt when it hands a task to a worker and returns the attempt id and generation in its result, and the release paths close it. The close path is shared, so route it through the existing release routing rather than duplicating logic: tools/releaseTask.ts, deregisterWorker.ts and the worker purge in state/workerStore.ts all end the attempt they own.

Not in scope: the finalizing phase, restart reconciliation and heartbeat changes; each is its own sibling task. Do not change which statuses are claimable or the existing nextStatusForRelease routing.

Depends on the attempt store and the fencing guard.

Verification: npx vitest run src/tools/claimNextTask.test.ts src/tools/releaseTask.test.ts from packages/moe-daemon.
definitionOfDone: claim_next_task opens an attempt for the claimed task and returns its id and generation in the tool result
release_task, deregister_worker and the worker purge each close the attempt they own, leaving no attempt in phase running for an unassigned task
A second claim of the same task after a release opens generation N+1 rather than reusing the closed attempt
Existing claim behaviour is unchanged: claimable statuses, alreadyAssigned resume, dependency gating and nextStatusForRelease routing all keep their current test coverage green
New cases cover claim-opens, release-closes and the generation increment
npx vitest run src/tools/claimNextTask.test.ts src/tools/releaseTask.test.ts passes and npm test in packages/moe-daemon stays green
taskRails: Do not change claimable statuses, dependency gating or nextStatusForRelease routing.
Attempt closing must go through one shared helper, not three copies.

implementationPlan.description: ADD THE ONE SHARED CLOSE HELPER. A task rail forbids three copies of the closing logic, so add a single exported function to packages/moe-daemon/src/state/attemptStore.ts — the store is where it belongs, and every release site already has a StateManager handle. It takes the state and a task id, reads `currentAttempt`, returns null when the task has no non-closed attempt, and otherwise moves that attempt to the closed phase through the existing `setAttemptPhase`, returning the closed record. Two properties matter and both need a comment saying why: it is idempotent, because an exit trap and a purge can both fire for the same task and a second call must be a no-op rather than an error; and it is tolerant of a task that never had an attempt, because every row created before this feature has none and a release of one must not start failing. Do not add a transition table, do not touch the generation, and do not delete records — a closed attempt is the history the generation counter depends on, since generations are allocated over every prior attempt including closed ones. Keep the store's existing write-then-publish ordering by reusing setAttemptPhase rather than writing directly.
implementationPlan.note: Added the ONE shared close helper `closeOpenAttempts(state, taskId): Promise<ExecutionAttempt[]>` after setAttemptPhase in state/attemptStore.ts (+35/-1, CRLF preserved, no diagnostics). Never deletes, never touches generation, no transition table; every close goes through setAttemptPhase so the store's write-then-publish order holds and a failed write throws with the attempt still published as open (caller decides fatality). ONE DELIBERATE DEVIATION from the step text: it closes EVERY non-closed attempt of the task and returns the closed records (empty array = nothing open) instead of closing only currentAttempt() and returning one-or-null — a release gives the seat up, so no open attempt may survive, and currentAttempt() names only the highest if a restored backup ever left two open (test 'release_task closes every open attempt of the task, not only the newest' pins this). implementationPlan.description: OPEN THE ATTEMPT ON THE CLAIM PATH AND RETURN IT. In packages/moe-daemon/src/tools/claimNextTask.ts, immediately AFTER the assignment write at line 278 succeeds and inside the same exclusive section, open the attempt for the claimed task. The ordering is deliberate and must be commented: the attempt is opened after the assignment, not before, because the assignment write is an optimistic race and an attempt opened by the loser would sit in the running phase and make the winner's open fail with ATTEMPT_ALREADY_OPEN — the loser must leave nothing behind. Fill the store's required fields from what the claim actually knows: the claiming worker id for both the worker and the runner identity, and the project root as the workspace, each with a comment that a distinct runner identity and per-attempt workspace arrive with the later reattachment work and are deliberately not invented here. Error handling has three arms. If the open refuses with ATTEMPT_ALREADY_OPEN and the open attempt belongs to this same worker, adopt it and return its id and generation — that is a resume, not a second execution. If it belongs to a worker that no longer holds the task, close it through the shared helper and open a fresh one, which is the crash-recovery path that produces the next generation. Any other failure is fatal to the claim: best-effort compensate by clearing the assignment you just wrote, inside its own try/catch so a failed compensation cannot mask the original error, then rethrow — a claim that cannot record its attempt is exactly the silent state this epic exists to remove. Add the attempt id and generation to the successful result object near line 429 as a sibling of the task object, not inside it, since that object mirrors the persisted task shape. Change nothing about claimable statuses, the alreadyAssigned resume, dependency gating or ranking; the resume path returns before the assignment write and must therefore open nothing.

comments.author: governor-983e1bae
comments.content:
GOVERNOR NOTE — read before wiring the guard into claim/release. The guard you depend on (task-a135d4d6, assertAttemptCurrent in util/enforcement.ts) made two behavioral decisions beyond its plan's literal text. Both are tested and correct, but your wiring must respect them or it will refuse legitimate calls.

1. NO UNASSIGNED-TASK EARLY RETURN. A caller presenting an attempt identity against an UNASSIGNED task is refused. The intent is right: a released task must not let a zombie back in. The consequence for you: never call assertAttemptCurrent in a release handler AFTER the task has been unassigned. Fence first, then unassign. Order matters, and getting it backwards will refuse every release.

2. CLOSED ATTEMPTS ARE REFUSED, NOT TOLERATED. A task whose attempts all exist but are CLOSED is refused. Only a task with NO attempt record at all gets the legacy tolerance (listAttempts().length === 0). So once your claim path opens an attempt and your release path closes it, that task is fenced from then on. Nothing falls back to "no current attempt = allow". If a test of yours expects a post-release mutation to pass, the test is wrong, not the guard.

Also: generation must be POSITIVE. 0 is INVALID_INPUT, matching the attempt store's floor of 1. Do not seed attempts at generation 0.

Source: worker-de4739a8's REVIEW handoff on task-a135d4d6, 2026-09-11 10:27. If QA changes any of this before DONE, the guard's final code wins over this note. Re-read enforcement.ts at your step 1.

planSizeWarnings: Plan touches 7 distinct files (target <=5); plans over 10 are rejected. Small file-disjoint tasks review better and parallelize.

planningNotes.approachesConsidered: (1) Opening the attempt BEFORE the assignment write, which is the epic's durable-first ordering — rejected after reading the store: the assignment is an optimistic race, and an attempt opened by the loser would sit in the running phase and make the WINNER's open fail with ATTEMPT_ALREADY_OPEN. Opening after the write is the only ordering that cannot poison another claimer, and the missing-attempt window is repaired by the adopt/close recovery arms on the next claim. (2) Closing the attempt inside each of the four release sites directly — forbidden by a task rail and genuinely worse, since the idempotence and the no-attempt tolerance would then need four copies. (3) Putting the shared helper in a new module — rejected: it is store logic, every caller already holds a StateManager, and the store file is where the write-then-publish ordering lives. (4) Deleting attempt records on close — rejected outright: generations are allocated as the maximum over EVERY prior attempt including closed ones, so deleting a record would reissue a generation an in-flight caller still believes is exclusively its own, which is the exact failure a fencing token prevents. (5) Adding runnerId and workspace as new tool arguments — rejected as speculative: the store requires both non-blank, so the claim fills them from what it knows and a comment points at the later reattachment task. (6) Failing the claim outright when the attempt cannot be opened — kept only for unexpected errors, with a best-effort compensating unassign, because the two known refusals have honest recoveries.

Named refusals to handle: ATTEMPT_ALREADY_OPEN, ATTEMPT_ID_TASK_MISMATCH, ATTEMPT_CLOSED, ATTEMPT_NOT_FOUND, ATTEMPT_GENERATION_EXHAUSTED. StateManager declares the attempts map at line 370 and loads it at line 1044. There are FOUR sites that unassign a task, not three: releaseTask.ts:250, workerLifecycle.ts:133 inside deregisterWorker, and workerStore.ts at 263 (worker deletion) and 347 (purgeAllWorkers). The task description names src/tools/deregisterWorker.ts, but that file is a 42-line delegator whose logic lives in workerLifecycle.ts — flagged in step 1 so QA is not surprised by the file list. purgeAllWorkers builds its updated task by hand instead of going through updateTask and deliberately keeps a per-worker try/catch so one bad record cannot abort startup. The claim assigns at claimNextTask.ts:278 inside runExclusive and builds its result near line 429, where the task object mirrors the persisted shape, so the attempt belongs beside it rather than inside it. Neither src/tools/deregisterWorker.test.ts nor src/state/workerStore.test.ts exists, which is why the deregister and purge cases go into releaseTask.test.ts — the file this task's verification command actually names.
planningNotes.risks: Seven distinct files is the floor, not scope creep: the task itself names four release call sites, the store helper has one home, and the verification command names two test files. The claim path is the dangerous edit — the resume path returns before the assignment write and must open nothing, or every idle wrapper poll would burn a generation. Closing must key on the seat being given up, not on where nextStatusForRelease routed the task, and must NOT fire on the blocked-hold or resource-grant paths, where the worker keeps its seat and therefore its attempt. The startup purge runs before any wrapper reconnects and must keep its per-worker error handling, or one unwritable attempt record aborts fleet startup. A closed attempt must never be deleted, since generation allocation reads every prior record. Assert exact generations and phases in tests; a truthiness assertion passes against a reused record. Finally, do not overstate the result: an attempt record fences daemon mutations only and cannot stop an already-running external CLI from writing shared files, which the epic's own architecture notes say out loud.
